answers.answer: Keep four tokens of each gem color and all five gold tokens; reveal three nobles. Remove unrevealed nobles from the game permanently.
answers.evidence: Token Adjustments: 2 players | 4 (remove 3 of each color) | 5 | 3. Setup: 'Remove remaining noble tiles from the game -- they will not be used.'

answers.answer: Three players use five gems per color, five gold and four nobles. Four players use seven gems per color, five gold and five nobles: two more gems per color, unchanged gold, and one more noble.
answers.evidence: Token Adjustments by Player Count lists 3 | 5 | 5 | 4 and 4 | 7 | 5 | 5.

answers.answer: Shuffle the three level decks separately and place them in a column with level 1 at bottom, level 2 in the middle and level 3 on top. Reveal four cards per level, a 3x4 market. The youngest player starts and play goes clockwise.
answers.evidence: Setup steps 1–3: 'Shuffle each ... separately'; 'Level 1 at bottom, Level 2 in middle, Level 3 on top'; 'Reveal 4 cards ... from each level'. First Player: 'The youngest player goes first. Play proceeds clockwise.'

answers.answer: Choose exactly one: take three different-colored gems; take two same-colored gems; reserve one development and take one gold if available; or buy one development. You cannot take gems then buy, or reserve then buy that card, on the same turn because each would combine two actions.
answers.evidence: Turn Structure: 'must perform exactly one of the following four actions' followed by those four choices.

answers.answer: Unsupported: the summary does not state what information about owned tokens must be visible or when it must be visible.
answers.evidence: The Token Hand Limit section describes the ten-token limit, but gives no token-visibility rule. The visibility requirement under Purchase a Development Card applies to cards.

answers.answer: You may take two green from four, leaving two. You cannot take two red from three. Check for at least four tokens in that color's supply when taking them, before removing the two. Neither gem-taking action may take gold.
answers.evidence: Take 2: 'at least 4 tokens ... in the supply when the player takes them'; 'If ... 3 or fewer ... cannot take 2'. Both gem actions say 'You may not take gold tokens with this action.'

answers.answer: Yes, you can temporarily reach twelve, then must immediately return two to end with ten. You may return newly drawn gems, and gold counts toward the ten-token limit.
answers.evidence: Token Hand Limit: 'including gold'; 'If taking tokens causes a player to exceed 10, they must immediately return tokens of their choice ... exactly 10'; 'may return tokens they just took'.

answers.answer: Reserve the card and take one available gold, temporarily reaching eleven tokens, then return one token of your choice, potentially that gold, to reach ten. If gold is empty, you may still reserve and receive no gold, so you remain at ten tokens.
answers.evidence: Reserve: 'also take 1 gold token'; 'If no gold tokens remain, you may still reserve ... but receive no gold'. Token Hand Limit permits returning 'tokens they just took'.

answers.answer: Reserve a face-up market card or the top card of any level deck. A card reserved from a deck is not shown to opponents. Only its reserving player may buy it.
answers.evidence: Reserve: 'A face-up development card from the 3x4 grid' or 'The top card from any one of the three level decks, without revealing it'; 'Reserved cards may only be purchased by the player who reserved them.'

answers.answer: No: at three reserved cards you cannot reserve again, even just to obtain gold. You cannot discard or exchange a reserved card to make room; purchasing it is the only way it leaves your hand.
answers.evidence: Reserved Cards: 'If a player already has 3, they cannot reserve another'; 'The only way to remove a reserved card from your hand is to purchase it.'

answers.answer: Immediately refill the reserved level-2 market card's space with the top card of the level-2 deck. Purchasing a face-up card uses the same replacement process. Buying a reserved card creates no market gap and causes no market replacement. If the relevant deck is empty, a vacated market space remains empty for the rest of the game.
answers.evidence: Card Replacement: 'Whenever a face-up card is acquired (purchased) or reserved from the grid, it is immediately replaced by the top card of the same level’s deck'; 'If the corresponding deck is empty, the empty space ... remains empty for the rest of the game.'

answers.answer: Spend one green token, or one gold substituting for that green; no blue tokens are needed. If bonuses cover all costs, spend no tokens. Bonuses are permanent and are not spent.
answers.evidence: Payment rules give this exact example: '2 blue ... 1 green ... 2 blue bonuses ... only need to spend 1 green token'; gold substitutes for any single gem; enough bonuses allow purchase 'without spending any tokens at all'; bonuses are permanent.

answers.answer: Yes. After bonuses, the cost is one blue, one black and one white. Spend the blue token for blue and one gold each for black and white. Return all three spent tokens to the supply. Your bonus cards stay with you and retain their permanent bonuses.
answers.evidence: Payment rules: bonuses reduce the tokens needed; 'Gold tokens ... can substitute for any single gem token'; spent gems and gold return to supply. Bonus Stacking: each purchased card adds a bonus 'permanently'.

answers.answer: Buy a face-up market development or a previously reserved development from your own hand. Put purchased developments face-up before you, sorted by bonus color and staggered so all players can see bonuses and prestige point values at all times.
answers.evidence: Purchase: 'a face-up development card from the grid or a previously reserved card from your hand'; 'face-up in front of you, sorted by bonus color and staggered so that bonuses and prestige point values are visible to all players at all times'.

answers.answer: You do not qualify with only two white bonuses; neither a white nor a gold token counts. A third white bonus qualifies you, with eligibility checked at turn end. Having bonuses above any required amount does not disqualify you.
answers.evidence: Noble Visits: 'at least the quantity and types of bonuses ... shown'; 'bonuses only ... not gem tokens'. Noble Tile Mechanics: 'having more is fine'.

answers.answer: Choose one noble; you cannot take both or decline all. The visit uses no action and gives three prestige points. Eligibility is checked at the end of your turn after your action and token-limit check.
answers.evidence: Noble Visits: 'automatic ... cannot refuse'; 'not an action'; multiple nobles: 'choose one'; 'at most one noble per turn'; '3 prestige points'. Turn Structure places the token-limit check before the noble check.

answers.answer: Unsupported: the summary does not state where a received noble tile is placed or whether it is face-up or hidden.
answers.evidence: Noble Visits explains receiving a noble and its points, but provides no tile-placement or face-up/hidden instruction.

answers.answer: C and D still take their turns. A takes no additional turn, leaving all four with equal turn counts. B is not guaranteed to win; the highest prestige total at the round's end wins, so another player may surpass B.
answers.evidence: End-Game Trigger: 'current round is completed so that every player has played the same number of turns'; End-of-Game Clarifications: trigger player 'may not necessarily win if another player surpasses them in the same final round'.

answers.answer: Your total becomes sixteen. This triggers the end because reaching fifteen or more qualifies, including by a noble visit. Complete the current round, then determine the winner by total prestige and the stated tiebreaker if needed.
answers.evidence: Noble tiles give '3 each'; End-Game Trigger: '15 or more prestige points'; Determining the Winner: 'most prestige points at the end of the final round'; noble points count.

answers.answer: B wins: A and B tie for the highest prestige at sixteen, and B's nine purchased developments beat A's ten. C's fewer developments cannot overcome having fewer prestige points. Nobles count toward prestige. B's three still-reserved cards are not purchased developments and do not count for that tiebreaker.
answers.evidence: Determining the Winner: 'most prestige points'; 'Noble tile points count toward the total'. Tiebreaker: 'fewest development cards' purchased. Reserved Cards distinguishes cards still in hand from purchasing them.
